title: World War II: The Home Front
summary: Trace how World War II reshaped the American home front across four systems — political, economic, social-cultural, and geographic — and weigh who benefited and who bore the costs.
challenge: World War II was fought overseas, but it transformed life inside the United States. The war remade American politics, the economy, society and culture, and where people lived — and it did so unevenly. Follow the war's shockwaves outward through four systems, weigh who benefited and who bore the costs, and decide which change left the deepest mark.

event.title: The U.S. Home Front in World War II

paths.immediateKey: Federal declarations of war and a rapid expansion of federal power — new war agencies, the draft, and censorship coordination.
paths.secondaryKey: Executive Order 9066 (1942) authorized the incarceration of Japanese Americans, while Executive Order 8802 (1941) created the Fair Employment Practices Committee — government now directly shaping civil rights and civil liberties.
paths.evidenceKey: Executive Order 9066; Korematsu v. United States (1944); Executive Order 8802.

paths.immediateKey: Industry converted to war production; deficit spending and war contracts ended the Depression and drove near-full employment; rationing managed scarce goods.
paths.secondaryKey: Postwar prosperity and an expanding middle class, fueled by wartime savings, war bonds, and the 1944 GI Bill.
paths.evidenceKey: ~300,000 aircraft and 86,000 tanks produced; OPA ration books; the GI Bill of 1944.

paths.immediateKey: Women entered war industries in large numbers ('Rosie the Riveter'); propaganda and shared sacrifice mobilized civilian culture.
paths.secondaryKey: Wartime experience reshaped expectations for women and minorities and seeded postwar civil-rights momentum (the 'Double V' campaign).
paths.evidenceKey: ~3 million women in defense plants; War Manpower Commission and OWI posters; the Tuskegee Airmen and Navajo Code Talkers.

paths.immediateKey: Massive internal migration to war-production centers (the West Coast, Detroit, the Gulf Coast), causing housing shortages and crowding.
paths.secondaryKey: Lasting demographic shifts — growth of the West and Sunbelt, permanent urbanization of Black and Latino populations, and the forced relocation of Japanese Americans to remote inland camps.
paths.evidenceKey: Continuation of the Great Migration; camps such as Manzanar (California) and Topaz (Utah); wartime 'boomtowns.'

mapData.benefitedKey: Industrial workers and the previously unemployed (jobs, higher wages); women and minorities gaining new (if temporary) economic footholds; returning veterans (the GI Bill); defense industries, farmers, and the broader postwar economy.
mapData.costKey: Japanese Americans — about 120,000 incarcerated under EO 9066, losing homes, businesses, and liberty; combat casualties and Gold Star families; consumers under rationing; and Black and other minority workers who still faced discrimination and segregation despite the FEPC.
mapData.greatestKey: Of the home front's effects — a wartime economy that ended the Depression, new opportunities for women and minorities, expanded federal power, or the incarceration of Japanese Americans — which mattered most in shaping the United States? Use specific evidence to defend which had the deepest or most lasting impact, and for whom.

teacherText.keyideas: WWII transformed the home front across systems: expanded federal power (war agencies, the draft, but also EO 9066 and the FEPC); a war economy that ended the Depression and built the postwar middle class (GI Bill); new but temporary openings for women and minorities; and large internal migrations that reshaped where Americans lived. Costs and benefits fell unevenly — most starkly on the ~120,000 Japanese Americans incarcerated under EO 9066.
teacherText.misconceptions:
• The war economy, not the New Deal alone, ended the Great Depression.
• New opportunities for women and minorities were real but often rolled back after 1945.
• The GI Bill's benefits were unevenly accessible — many Black veterans were effectively excluded.
teacherText.vocabulary: Arsenal of Democracy, rationing, Executive Order 9066, internment/incarceration, Rosie the Riveter, GI Bill, FEPC, Double V.
teacherText.context: Pearl Harbor Dec. 7, 1941; EO 8802 (1941); EO 9066 (Feb. 19, 1942); ~120,000 Japanese Americans incarcerated; ~3 million women in defense plants; GI Bill 1944; V-E and V-J Day 1945.
